ao_demand_evidence.input: Suggest a three-member food chain from these observations: beetle larvae eat grass roots, a small lizard eats the larvae, and another beetle feeds on dead wood. Show the direction of energy transfer.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Grass → beetle larva → lizard.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Describe the energy budget of a consumer by calculating the energy that remains in new biomass when 500 kJ is eaten, 150 kJ is egested and 300 kJ is transferred to the surroundings through respiration, with no other changes.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: 500 − 150 − 300 = 50 kJ remains in new biomass. Most of the energy eaten, 450 kJ, leaves by egestion and respiration, so only 10% is stored.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A producer base provides 1000 kJ per year and each transfer to the next level keeps 20% of the energy. A consumer population needs at least 30 kJ per year. Explain why the first two consumer levels could be supported but the third could not.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The energy available is 200 kJ, then 40 kJ, then 8 kJ. The first two are above 30 kJ and the third is below it, so the third level cannot be supported.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Fig. VIS-6116-5.1-14 is a pyramid of biomass for a grassland. Its bars show dry mass per square metre of 800 g for producers, 80 g for primary consumers, 12 g for secondary consumers and 2 g for tertiary consumers. Describe the pattern in the pyramid and state one limit on what it shows.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The biomass falls at each level from 800 g/m² for producers to 2 g/m² for tertiary consumers, so the pyramid narrows strongly upwards. It is a snapshot of standing mass, so it does not by itself show how much energy is transferred in a year.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A harvest of an edible crop provides 9000 MJ of food energy if people eat it directly. If the crop is instead fed to livestock and the livestock are eaten, it provides only 900 MJ. Explain why the direct route is more efficient.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: 9000 ÷ 900 = 10, so ten times as much food energy is available by the direct route. The livestock route has an extra trophic level, where energy is transferred as heat in respiration and lost in material that is not eaten or is egested.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A model atmosphere was in balance before fuel burning began. Burning now adds 9 carbon units a year, and natural uptake has risen by 6 units a year in response. Suggest the annual net change and why extra uptake alone does not give a balanced system.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The net change is 9 − 6 = +3 units a year. Uptake has risen but is still less than the added release, so carbon keeps accumulating in the atmosphere.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A cleared forest held 100 carbon units. New seedlings planted there hold 2 units and take up 1 unit a year. Suggest why planting them does not immediately replace the carbon that was removed.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The seedlings hold only 2 of the 100 units that were removed. Uptake of 1 unit a year is a rate, so the store builds up only over many years of growth.

ao_demand_evidence.input: In a model, warm soil releases more carbon dioxide when it is moist but almost none after severe drying. Suggest why warming alone cannot decide whether the soil releases more carbon dioxide.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Decomposers need water as well as warmth. When the soil is severely dry their activity almost stops, so moisture, not temperature alone, decides whether warming leads to more carbon dioxide release.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Fig. VIS-6116-5.3-05 is a graph of population size against time for a population with limited resources. The curve is S-shaped, rising steeply in the middle and then levelling off at a high population size. Explain the difference between the steep region and the level region.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: In the steep region births are much greater than deaths, so the population grows quickly while resources are plentiful. In the level region limiting factors such as food or space mean that additions and removals are about equal, so the population size stays roughly constant.

ao_demand_evidence.input:
Fig. VIS-6116-5.3-08 is a graph of the data in the table, for a model town. The total population rises each year while the percentage growth rate falls. Suggest why the total population keeps rising while the percentage growth rate falls.

| Year | Population | Growth rate in the year (%) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 20 000 | not applicable |
| 1 | 21 000 | 5.0 |
| 2 | 21 840 | 4.0 |
| 3 | 22 386 | 2.5 |
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The growth rate falls from 5.0% to 2.5%, but the population rises each year from 20 000 to 22 386, adding 1000, 840 and 546 people. A smaller percentage of a larger population still adds people, so the total keeps rising, but more slowly.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A district grows enough grain overall, but 30% spoils in storage and remote households cannot reach the markets. Suggest why improving storage and transport may help more than clearing more habitat for crops.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The district already grows enough, so the shortage comes from spoilage and poor access, not from too small a harvest. Better storage and transport make the existing food available and avoid removing more habitat.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two slopes receive equal heavy rain. One has been cleared and the other keeps its roots and ground cover. Explain why the stream below the cleared slope may become muddier.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The cleared slope has no ground cover to break the force of the rain and no roots to bind the soil. More soil is loosened and washed into the stream, so it carries more sediment even though the rainfall is the same.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A region has full grain stores, but the bridges to three villages are destroyed. Explain why a food surplus for the region does not rule out severe shortage in those villages.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The destroyed bridges stop the grain reaching the villages. The regional surplus is not the same as the food that the villagers can actually obtain.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two drought-affected districts lose equal amounts of harvest, but one has food reserves and funded distribution. Explain why equal crop loss need not lead to equal famine risk.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The reserves and distribution replace the lost local supply in one district. This protection breaks the link between crop loss and food shortage there.

ao_demand_evidence.input: After a flood, undamaged grain is stored in a town 60 km away. Households had about one week of food at home, and the only road to the town has been closed for five weeks. Explain why households may still face food shortage even though no grain was damaged.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The closed road stops the grain being delivered, so food is available but households cannot reach it. Their food at home lasted only about a week, so it ran out long before the road reopened.

ao_demand_evidence.input: The accessible food in a model district rises by 10% while its population rises by 25%. Explain why more total food does not mean more food per person.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The population rises faster than the food total. Dividing the new supply by the larger population gives 1.10 ÷ 1.25 = 0.88, so each person has about 12% less than before.

ao_demand_evidence.input: The grain stocks in a market stay constant while the price of grain doubles. A household's income does not change. Explain why the household's food security may worsen even though the harvest has not fallen.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The same income buys half as much grain at double the price. The price rise reduces the household's access to food even though total production is unchanged.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Collected plastic bottles are piled on open ground beside a river and left there. Suggest why this is not recycling and may still pollute the river.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Recycling means the bottles are processed into new material, but here they are only stored. Rain and wind can wash the bottles back into the river, so the pollution risk is still there.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A farmer grows a legume crop and then removes all the above-ground material from the field at harvest. Suggest why the next crop will not receive all the nitrogen that the legume fixed.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Much of the fixed nitrogen is in the plant tissue that was removed. Most of the benefit to the next crop comes from material that stays in the field and decomposes.

ao_demand_evidence.input: During a litter survey, a plastic bag breaks into small pieces, but the total mass of plastic is unchanged. Suggest why a fall in the number of whole bags does not show that the plastic has biodegraded.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The change observed is fragmentation, not breakdown by living organisms. The total mass is unchanged, so the pieces remain, and counting whole bags gives a false picture.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A mountain species needs cool habitat. Warming has pushed it uphill, but it now lives at the summit and there is no higher cool area. Explain why moving uphill, which helped before, can no longer protect it.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: As warming continues, the summit itself becomes too warm for the species, and there is no higher, cooler land to move to. Its survival and reproduction then fall.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A wetland species has plenty of food in nearby grassland, but drainage destroys the only pools where it breeds. Explain why plentiful food does not prevent its decline.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Without the pools the species cannot breed, so no young are produced. Adults that die are not replaced, and the population declines however much food there is.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two streams have the same amount of fish food. One receives organic waste and often has very low dissolved oxygen. Explain why extra food would not prevent fish declining in that stream.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Microorganisms breaking down the organic waste use up the dissolved oxygen. Fish need oxygen for respiration, so they cannot survive there even though food is available.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A model animal population produces five surviving young a year but loses eight breeding adults a year to poaching, with all other changes balanced. Explain why having a stable habitat does not mean the population is stable.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The removal of eight is greater than the five young added, so the population falls by three a year. Protecting the habitat does not stop this loss of adults.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A count rises from 12 to 20 animals while the survey effort rises from two to ten days. Explain why this does not show that the population is recovering.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The extra survey effort can explain the higher count, because more days give more sightings. Animals seen per day fell from 6 to 2, so the counts must be compared for equal effort.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A reserve contains dry-season grazing but excludes the only dry-season water source. Explain why it may fail to conserve a herbivore.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: In the dry season the herbivores cannot reach water, which they need to survive. Grazing alone does not meet all their habitat needs, so they may leave or die.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A community has no waste collection. Explain why many anti-litter posters may not reduce the waste in the river.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Without collection, people have nowhere to put the waste, so they cannot act on the message. Education works only when people have a practical alternative.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Many captive-bred animals are released into the same unprotected habitat where their parents were lost. Explain why this may fail to restore the population.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The released animals face the same threat, such as poaching or habitat loss, so many die before they breed. Adding animals does not remove the cause of the decline.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A seed bank stores a thousand seeds from a single parent plant. Explain why this does not necessarily conserve the genetic variety of the whole plant population.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Seeds from one parent carry only that plant's genes, which are a small part of the variety in the population. Seeds should be collected from many parents, because the number of seeds is not the same as genetic variety.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A model reserve earns N$120 per visitor for conservation, but nesting success falls when there are more than 40 visitors a day. Option X allows 80 visitors a day and option Y allows 40 at the same fee. Suggest why the higher daily income of option X is not enough reason to choose it.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Option X earns N$9600 a day compared with N$4800 for Y, but it goes beyond the nesting limit of 40 visitors. Poor breeding would harm the wildlife that tourism depends on, so income must be judged together with the biological cost.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A model orchard can buy replacement trees, but the habitat of its pollinating insects is being removed. Explain why protecting that habitat may help fruit production more than planting more trees alone.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Fruit forms only after flowers are pollinated, and the orchard depends on insects for this. Extra trees without pollinators will not produce more fruit, so protecting pollinator habitat helps production more.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Tourist bookings fell after recorded poaching increased, but the main access road closed at the same time. Suggest why this does not show how much of the fall was caused by poaching.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The road closure could reduce visits by itself. The two changes happened together, so the effect of poaching cannot be separated unless access is taken into account.

Carbon-stock and annual-flow distinctions are explicit; more uptake alone is not balance.
Extinction cause explanations are taught independently; definition evidence is not represented as testing the causal route.
